# Broken-glass reference photographs

A set of real photographs and real traced fracture patterns, for visual comparison only. None of these are to be used on the website. Compiled 2 October 2026 for the OnySnow Studios broken-glass effect, as a companion to `fracture-physics.md`.

**How entries are written**

- Each entry gives the source link, licence and author as stated on the source page, then one line on what the picture shows and why it is useful.
- **`refs/…`** marks a small copy (up to about 1,000 px) saved in `research/refs/`. `refs/index.md` maps each file to its source, author and licence.
- Licences are copied from the source page. "Pexels License", "Pixabay Content License" and the Unsplash License are the sites' own free licences, not Creative Commons.
- **Glass type.** Most photos do not say whether the glass is annealed, laminated or tempered. I give the type only where the source states it ("stated") or the picture plainly shows it. Otherwise it says "type not stated".
- Every Wikimedia Commons, Pexels and Pixabay picture listed was looked at, as a thumbnail or larger. The few marked **(not viewed)** are listed from their page text only.
- I left out pictures whose subject is a fatal attack or a death, even where the glass detail was useful.

## 1. Impact stars in plain window glass, close and wide

- **`refs/cat-01-star-wide-missing-centre.jpg`** — [Durban Is Shattered](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Durban_Is_Shattered_(183437978).jpg). CC BY-SA 2.0; Chris Bloom. A window in a shopping centre with about 30 long, nearly straight radials from a crushed centre where pieces are missing. A few short concentric segments sit close to the centre. **The best wide star**: note the irregular angular spacing and how few rings there are.
- **`refs/cat-01-small-star-near-frame.jpg`** — [Crack on window 20180404](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Crack_on_window_20180404.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Santeri Viinamäki. A small, low-energy star of 4 to 5 slightly curved legs in a domestic window pane, one leg running to the frame. Shows what a light tap really gives.
- **`refs/cat-01-star-door-glass.jpg`** — [Köln wikicon 2014 008](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:K%C3%B6ln_wikicon_2014_008.jpg). CC BY-SA 3.0; atamari. A large glazed door with a fine star of about 35 radials from an impact near the floor. Hardly any rings or forks, and the cracks are seen mainly by reflection. Type not stated; probably laminated, since it is not diced.
- **`refs/cat-01-star-near-frame-crushed.jpg`** — [Day 195 – Shut the burglar out](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Day_195_-_Shut_the_burglar_out_(9293361460).jpg). CC BY-SA 2.0; West Midlands Police. A close-up of many radials converging on a crushed spot beside a window frame bar. The radial edges glint white.
- **`refs/cat-01-star-hole-window-pexels.jpg`** — [Hole in broken glass](https://www.pexels.com/photo/hole-in-broken-glass-15156848/). Pexels License; Ivars. A window pane with a hole, about 25 radials, short concentric links near the hole, and dagger tips around the hole's rim.
- **`refs/cat-01-star-small-web-pexels.jpg`** — [Broken glass on wooden surface](https://www.pexels.com/photo/broken-glass-on-wooden-surface-3703737/). Pexels License; Lisa Fotios. A dark window with a dense star and a tight web of concentric segments around the impact. A detached shard lies to the right.
- [Broken Glass (18434524128)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_Glass_(18434524128).jpg). CC BY 2.0; Rodrigo Paredes. Black-and-white close-up of a star of about 15 radials, some forking, with a few concentric links.
- [Köln wikicon 2014 007](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:K%C3%B6ln_wikicon_2014_007.jpg). CC BY-SA 3.0; atamari. The same door at night: the star is visible only where it catches the light.
- [Daneben](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Daneben_(5421642393).jpg). CC BY-SA 2.0; tiegeltuf. A window with a bird-warning sticker and a radial star beside it, black and white.
- [Close-up of shattered glass against blue sky](https://www.pexels.com/photo/close-up-of-shattered-glass-against-blue-sky-39168071/). Pexels License; Irina Rodrigues. See category 4.
- [Broken glass](https://www.pexels.com/photo/broken-glass-7049027/). Pexels License; Praksh. A thin, sparse star of about 10 radials from a tiny cone, on a dark background.
- [Brocken glass](https://www.pexels.com/photo/brocken-glass-10164374/). Pexels License; Bruno Pires. A pane cut into large polygons by a few long cracks, with a small chunk near the junction. Shows how sparse a light break is.
- [A close up of a broken glass window](https://unsplash.com/photos/a-close-up-of-a-broken-glass-window-bjVuZJSrhUw). Unsplash License. **(not viewed)** Listed from Unsplash's alt text.

## 2. Cone and crater close-ups, both faces

- **`refs/cat-02-hertzian-cone-plug.jpg`** — [Herzian cone](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Herzian_cone.jpg). CC BY-SA 3.0; Polyparadigm. "A Herzian cone fracture in glass, from the Downtown Cafe in Merced, CA". A cone-shaped plug knocked out of a pane, seen from the wide (exit) side, with the small entry hole at the apex. **Shows the true 3-D shape of the cone.**
- **`refs/cat-02-crater-spall-rings.jpg`** — [Hypervelocity impact damage on silica glass](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hypervelocity_impact_damage_on_silica_glass.jpg). CC0; Jasalem21. "Damage zones (crater, crush, petaloids)". From the centre out: a white crushed pit, a smooth conchoidal crater, then rings of scalloped spall flakes. The anatomy of a crater.
- **`refs/cat-02-bullet-hole-crater.jpg`** — [Bullet Hole](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bullet_Hole_(18365701419).jpg). CC BY 2.0; Tony Webster. A small hole in a downtown window, with a white flaked crater rim and only 2 to 3 radials, one of them long. Shows how *little* cracking a fast small projectile causes.
- **`refs/cat-02-bullet-hole-radials.jpg`** — [Bullet hole in a window of the gendarmerie in Cameroon](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bullet_hole_in_a_window_of_the_gendarmerie_in_Cameroon,_December_8,_2017.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Jules Emmanuel Ntap (VOA). A hole with a white crushed ring and radials running to long cracks.
- **`refs/cat-02-pellet-crater-flakes-pixabay-1.jpg`** — [Glass pane, broken, splintered](https://pixabay.com/photos/glass-pane-glass-broken-splintered-1497229/). Pixabay Content License; kirahoffmann. A pellet-sized hole in a window with a rosette of shell-shaped conchoidal flakes around it and about 8 radials starting at the crater rim. **Exactly the "spall flakes" layer.**
- **`refs/cat-02-pellet-crater-flakes-pixabay-2.jpg`** — [Glass pane, broken (1497227)](https://pixabay.com/photos/glass-pane-glass-broken-splintered-1497227/). Pixabay Content License; kirahoffmann. The same hole seen obliquely. The radial fracture faces glow green and the flakes stand proud.
- [Glass pane, broken (1497232)](https://pixabay.com/photos/glass-pane-glass-broken-splintered-1497232/) and [(1497233)](https://pixabay.com/photos/glass-pane-glass-broken-splintered-1497233/). Pixabay Content License; kirahoffmann. More angles on the same crater. In 1497233 the radial faces go dark and green depending on the angle.
- **`refs/cat-02-ring-cones-in-basalt.jpg`** — [Hertzian cone](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hertzian_cone.png). CC BY-SA 3.0; Eurico Zimbres. Ring-shaped Hertzian cone traces on basalt paving setts. Not glass, but it shows nested partial rings from repeated blunt contacts.
- [Lintong Xian China Huaqing-Pool-10](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lintong_Xian_China_Huaqing-Pool-10.jpg). CC BY-SA 3.0; CEphoto, Uwe Aranas. A historic (1936) bullet hole in a window pane kept in a frame, with radials and long cracks.
- [Shop window showing bullet hole, Petrograd 1917](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Shop_window_showing_bullet_hole,_riots_of_July_1917,_Petrograd_(St._Petersburg),_Russia_LCCN91789618.jpg). Public domain; Library of Congress. A wide shot of a large shop window with a hole and a radial star.
- [Sarajevo siege bullet holed window](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sarajevo_siege_bullet_holed_window.jpg). CC BY 3.0; Christian Maréchal. Black-and-white window with bullet holes, wide view.
- [A bullet hole in a glass](https://www.pexels.com/photo/a-bullet-hole-in-a-glass-21263452/). Pexels License; Pascal Bronsert. A round white crushed ring with fine radials in a shop window. Type not stated.
- Quinn, NIST SP 960-16e3, Fig. 6.39 (p. 6-43) and Fig. 6.36 (p. 6-39): real blunt-impact cones in glass plates, and profile sketches of cones at different speeds and angles. See category 16.

## 3. Crushed zone close-ups

- **`refs/cat-03-crushed-ring-sky.jpg`** — [Alboni street in Paris through a broken glass](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Alboni_street_in_Paris_throught_a_broken_glass.JPG). CC BY-SA 3.0; Oliver H. A broken shop window against the sky. A ring of pulverised white glass about the size of a coin, with 10 or more radials leaving it.
- **`refs/cat-03-crushed-crater-shuttle-window.jpg`** — [Space debris impact on Space Shuttle window](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Space_debris_impact_on_Space_Shuttle_window.jpg). Public domain; NASA. A white crushed and spalled crater left by a paint chip (STS-7), with a scale bar. The look of comminuted glass.
- **`refs/cat-03-crushed-impacts-armour-glass.jpg`** — [IDET2007 bulletproof glass](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IDET2007_bulletproof_glass.jpg). Public domain; Shaddack. Stated as laminated bullet-resistant glass after tests. Three impacts, each with a white crushed core and a star; the cracks between impacts link up.
- **`refs/cat-03-dense-star-crushed-centre-pexels.jpg`** — [Shattered glass pattern with radial cracks](https://www.pexels.com/photo/shattered-glass-pattern-with-radial-cracks-33530412/). Pexels License; Haberdoedas Photography. A very dense radial star with a large whitened crushed centre. Type not stated.
- [IDET2007 bulletproof glass armor](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IDET2007_bulletproof_glass_armor.jpg). Public domain; Shaddack. Stated as a 55.6 mm glass-polymer composite. Several impacts, with crushed white zones tens of millimetres across.
- **`refs/cat-13-hail-crushed-disc.jpg`** (listed in 13) — a hailstone crushed disc on a windscreen.
- **`refs/cat-13-windscreen-spiderweb.jpg`** (listed in 13) — a white crushed centre in a windscreen.

## 4. Radial and concentric crack detail

- **`refs/cat-04-radials-cross-cracks.jpg`** — [Shattered](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Shattered_-_Flickr_-_wburris.jpg). CC BY-SA 2.0; Bill Burris. **Key reference.** Long radial daggers cut into rows of short pieces by concentric cross-cracks. The segments are offset at each radial, never forming a smooth ring. Crack edges glint blue.
- **`refs/cat-04-radial-concentric-bw.jpg`** — [01 – VITE SPEZZATE](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:01_-_VITE_SPEZZATE.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Pinat1947. Black-and-white close-up of radials with staggered concentric links.
- **`refs/cat-04-radials-concentric-closeup-pexels.jpg`** — [Close-up of shattered glass against blue sky](https://www.pexels.com/photo/close-up-of-shattered-glass-against-blue-sky-39168071/). Pexels License; Irina Rodrigues. A close-up from near the impact, with a dense radial fan, short chords between neighbours and thin needle pieces.
- **`refs/cat-04-display-star-rings.jpg`** — [München, vandalised display](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:M%C3%BCnchen,_vandalisierter_%C3%96PNV-Bildschirm,_1.jpeg). CC0; Renardo la vulpo. A display cover glass with one impact: about 25 radials, two or three partial concentric arcs, and cracks reaching the frame. Type not stated.
- [BROKEN MIRROR pro](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BROKEN_MIRROR_pro.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Abass.Abdul.Wasi. A black-and-white mirror with a full spider web of radials and many concentric segments.
- [Broken painted mirror](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_painted_mirror_-_panoramio.jpg). CC BY 3.0; Jens Cederskjold. A radial star in a mirror with blue paint; the long straight radials are clear.
- [Starnberg, damaged display](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Starnberg,_Bildschirm_am_Bahnhof,_Vandalismus,_1.jpg). CC0; Renardo la vulpo. Three impact stars in one display glass. Cracks from the later impacts stop at the earlier cracks (T-junctions).
- [Pattern of broken glass](https://www.pexels.com/photo/pattern-of-broken-glass-15521643/) and [Cracks of a broken glass](https://www.pexels.com/photo/cracks-of-a-broken-glass-8307385/). Pexels License; Tom Van Dyck and Now1993. 15521643 is a diced, tempered-looking web (compare with category 15). 8307385 is a large pane with a radial and concentric web seen against a landscape; type not stated.
- **`refs/cat-08-fallen-pane-star.jpg`** (listed in 8) — a radial and concentric pattern on a pane lying on the ground.

## 5. Branching and fan cracks

- **`refs/cat-05-fan-from-edge-impact.jpg`** — [WTC Mattley 013](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:WTC_Mattley_013.JPG). CC BY-SA 3.0; Matthew & Lesley (Wikipedia Takes Coventry). **Key reference.** A fan of dozens of long radials spreading upward from an impact at the bottom edge. Near the impact they are dense, needle-thin and branching.
- **`refs/cat-05-fan-dense-curved-pixabay.jpg`** — [Glass pane, window, splintered](https://pixabay.com/photos/glass-pane-window-splintered-446857/). Pixabay Content License; martaposemuckel. A dense fan of gently curved, nearly parallel cracks crossing a whole pane from an off-picture origin.
- **`refs/cat-05-parallel-curved-cracks.jpg`** — [Broken glass door](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_glass_door.JPG). CC BY-SA 4.0; Fauvirt. Long parallel curved cracks on a glass door: the outer part of a fan, far from the origin. Type not stated.
- [Broken-Window-20130513](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken-Window-20130513.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; WiseWoman. "Security glass": a fan from a low impact, with curved cross-cracks. See category 13.
- **`refs/cat-01-star-near-frame-crushed.jpg`** (listed in 1) — branching radials near an impact.
- Quinn, NIST SP 960-16e3, Fig. 4.15 (p. 4-22): sketched fan arrays and inner and outer cross-cracks in disks broken at low, medium and high strength. See category 16.

## 6. Slivers, needles and daggers

- **`refs/cat-06-slivers-on-black-pexels.jpg`** — [Close-up shot of broken glass pieces on a black surface (9966691)](https://www.pexels.com/photo/close-up-shot-of-broken-glass-pieces-on-a-black-surface-9966691/). Pexels License; Dan Cristian Pădureț. About 15 slender slivers and daggers laid out on black, edges lit. **Shape catalogue for needles.**
- **`refs/cat-06-daggers-on-black-pexels.jpg`** — [Close-up of broken glass pieces on black (9966709)](https://www.pexels.com/photo/close-up-shot-of-broken-glass-pieces-on-a-black-surface-9966709/). Pexels License; Dan Cristian Pădureț. Eight long daggers, side by side, with jagged and curved edges.
- **`refs/cat-06-long-shards-edges-pexels.jpg`** — [Pieces of glass](https://www.pexels.com/photo/pieces-of-glass-7191404/). Pexels License; cottonbro studio. A pile of long, thick shards. Their fracture faces show as green bands along the edges.
- [Os últimos suspiros de um espelho quebrado](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Os_%C3%BAltimos_suspiros_de_um_espelho_quebrado_(12490136774).jpg) and [… II](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Os_%C3%BAltimos_suspiros_de_um_espelho_quebrado_II_(12489661635).jpg). CC BY 2.0; Cícero R. C. Omena. Long mirror daggers stuck upright in grass.
- [Bjorn7](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bjorn7.JPG). CC0; Stamboliyski. A gloved hand holding a long, thick excavated glass shard.
- [Toshiba MK1403MAV broken glass platter](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Toshiba_MK1403MAV_-_broken_glass_platter-93375.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Raimond Spekking. A glass hard-disk platter broken into radial wedges and slivers. A clean example of wedge shapes in a thin disc.
- [Smashed-Glass](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Smashed-Glass.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Qwerty1234qwer. Shards and slivers scattered on black.
- **`refs/cat-05-fan-from-edge-impact.jpg`** (listed in 5) — needles in the fan zone, still in place.

## 7. Small chunks and grit

- **`refs/cat-07-grit-macro-1.jpg`** — [Verre pilé, crushed glass on urban road, 03](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Verre_pil%C3%A9_Crushed_glass_on_urban_road_Lamiot_03.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Lamiot. Macro of glass crushed by traffic, "partly reduced to powder": angular grit from about 1 mm down to dust. It is bottle glass, so it is thick and coloured.
- **`refs/cat-07-grit-macro-scale.jpg`** — [Verre pilé 04](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Verre_pil%C3%A9_Crushed_glass_on_urban_road_Lamiot_04.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Lamiot. The same grit with ruled scale lines. **Gives real sizes for "sand-sized" particles.**
- [Verre pilé 05](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Verre_pil%C3%A9_Crushed_glass_on_urban_road_Lamiot_05.jpg) and [Verre pilé 01](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Verre_pil%C3%A9_Crushed_glass_on_urban_road_Lamiot_01.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Lamiot. More of the series; 05 shows a scale.
- **`refs/cat-07-small-chunks-soil.jpg`** — [Glassplitter Grünglas](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Glassplitter_Gr%C3%BCnglas.JPG). CC BY-SA 3.0; 4028mdk09. Hundreds of small, blocky green-glass chunks a few millimetres across on soil.
- **`refs/cat-07-small-shards-street.jpg`** — [Shattered glass (4409500248)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Shattered_glass_(4409500248).jpg). CC BY-SA 2.0; Kiran Jonnalagadda. A paved floor strewn with small shards and grit from broken glass doors, catching the light.
- [Broken glass on the road](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_glass_on_the_road.JPG). CC0; Georg Pik. Bottle-glass grit on asphalt.
- [Eventually, it all becomes sand](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Eventually,_it_all_becomes_sand_(6078163981).jpg). CC BY 2.0; waferboard. Worn glass bits among beach sand. Shows the finest end of the size range.
- [Close-up of shattered glass](https://www.pexels.com/photo/close-up-of-shattered-glass-5933614/). Pexels License; ericbvd. A heap of small angular shards, blue-tinted.

## 8. Fallen shards and debris on floors

- **`refs/cat-08-flat-shards-paving.jpg`** — [Broken glass, Belfast, April 2010](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_glass,_Belfast,_April_2010.JPG). CC BY-SA 3.0; Ardfern. **Key reference.** Big flat window-glass shards (daggers and polygons) lying on red paving. Each piece is slightly tilted and lit differently, and the edges show as green lines.
- **`refs/cat-08-shards-on-dirt.jpg`** — [Kistner-Bremerhaven-61](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kistner-Bremerhaven-61_hg.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Hannes Grobe. Flat triangular window shards of many sizes scattered on bare earth.
- **`refs/cat-08-shards-reflect-sky.jpg`** — [Three pieces of sky](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Three_pieces_of_sky_(33715637408).jpg). CC BY-SA 2.0; Egor Zhuravlev. Three flat shards on asphalt, each mirroring the sky. **How fallen glass catches light.**
- **`refs/cat-08-shards-on-ground-2.jpg`** — [زجاج مكسور 7](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%D8%B2%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AC_%D9%85%D9%83%D8%B3%D9%88%D8%B1_7.jpg). CC0; ديفيد عادل وهبة خليل. Window shards and grit scattered on dry ground.
- **`refs/cat-08-fallen-pane-star.jpg`** — [Broken window glass in Esbjerg, 3](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_window_glass_in_Esbjerg,_3.jpg). CC BY-SA 2.0; Kent Madsen. **Key reference.** A large pane lying on the ground with its whole radial pattern intact. Long daggers, short ring links near the impact, and loose pieces around it.
- [Esbjerg, 1](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_window_glass_in_Esbjerg,_1.jpg), [2](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_window_glass_in_Esbjerg,_2.jpg), [4](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_window_glass_in_Esbjerg,_4.jpg), [5](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_window_glass_in_Esbjerg,_5.jpg). CC BY-SA 2.0; Kent Madsen. Other views of the same fallen pane.
- **`refs/cat-08-single-shard-carpet.jpg`** — [Broken window glass on apartment floor after break-in by firefighters](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_window_glass_on_apartment_floor_after_break-in_by_firefighters_due_to_water_leak,_Paris_2004.jpg). CC0; Syced. One window shard on carpet. Its edge shows as a green line.
- **`refs/cat-08-thick-shard-sidewalk.jpg`** — [Glass debris on sidewalk, Atlanta storm](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Glass_debris_on_sidewalk_-_14_March_2008_Downtown_Atlanta_storm.JPG). CC BY-SA 4.0; Daniel Mayer. A thick tinted shard on concrete. A curved, conchoidal broken edge is visible.
- **`refs/cat-08-debris-layer-floor.jpg`** — [Cafe Pripyat interior, shattered glass on floor](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cafe_Pripyat_interior_shattered_glass_on_floor_from_ornate_windows_that_used_to_be_in_the_building_-_Pripyat_-_Ukraine.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Joël van der Loo. A thick layer of mixed coloured window glass covering a floor.
- **`refs/cat-08-shards-on-sill-pexels.jpg`** — [Broken window glass on windowsill](https://www.pexels.com/photo/broken-window-glass-on-windowsill-12348489/). Pexels License; Juan C. Palacios. Shards collected on the sill below a broken pane: the "falls straight down" debris.
- [Shattered glass (4408734447)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Shattered_glass_(4408734447).jpg). CC BY-SA 2.0; Kiran Jonnalagadda. Large pieces of a glass door lying flat on a floor, warm light.
- [Shattered glass (4408733953)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Shattered_glass_(4408733953).jpg). CC BY-SA 2.0; Kiran Jonnalagadda. Shards in a dark corridor, lit from one side.
- [زجاج مكسور 6](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%D8%B2%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AC_%D9%85%D9%83%D8%B3%D9%88%D8%B1_6.jpg). CC0; ديفيد عادل وهبة خليل. More shards on dry ground.
- [Sunset (greglobinski)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sunset_-_Flickr_-_greglobinski.jpg). CC BY 2.0; Greg Lobinski. Black-and-white broken window with fragments lying on the sill and floor.
- [Shattered light fixture 1](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Shattered_light_fixture_1.jpg). CC0; W. Carter. A glass dome broken on a bamboo mat. The scatter pattern shows big pieces near the fall point and small ones further out. Opal glass, not window glass.
- [1949 Althingi broken glass](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1949-althingi-broken-glass.jpg), [floor](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1949-althingi-broken-glass-floor.jpg), [floor pan](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1949-althingi-broken-glass-floor-pan.jpg). Public domain. Window glass on a parliament floor and carpet after a riot, black and white.
- [Kaputtes Schaufenster nach Fasching](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kaputtes_Schaufenster_nach_Fasching.JPG). CC0; Superwind. A broken shop window at night with debris spread across the floor inside.
- [Spiegel 001](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:001_2012_02_03_Spiegel.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Friedrich Haag. Mirror pieces on the floor.
- [Tunisia-12-serious glass](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tunisia-12-serious_glass_(6493871393).jpg). CC BY 2.0; Weldon Kennedy. Thick broken sheets and chunks on the ground.
- [Abandoned Schoolhouse, Pripyat 05](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Abandoned_Schoolhouse_-_Pripyat_Ghost_Town_-_Chernobyl_Exclusion_Zone_-_Northern_Ukraine_-_05_(26495584643).jpg). CC BY-SA 2.0; Adam Jones. Fallen window frames and glass among papers on a floor.

Pexels License; cottonbro studio. Shards on concrete and on black.
- [Glass broken destruction](https://pixabay.com/photos/glass-broken-destruction-cracks-5105871/). Pixabay Content License; Mitrey. Flat shards on a wet floor, teal edges.
- [Glass shard](https://pixabay.com/photos/glass-shard-of-glass-broken-shard-5745598/). Pixabay Content License; timoplatte. Small shards on dark ground with bokeh.

## 9. Pane edges, side faces and fracture surfaces

- **`refs/cat-09-fracture-surface-hackle.jpg`** — [Glass fracture](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Glass_fracture.jpg). CC BY-SA 2.5; Christopher Thomas. "The fractured edge of a broken drinking glass", seen edge-on. Feather and staircase hackle along a wavy crack. **What a fracture face looks like up close.**
- **`refs/cat-09-conchoidal-ribs.jpg`** — [Cassure conchoïdale](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cassure-conchoidale.jpg). CC BY-SA 3.0; no author given on the page. A shell-shaped (conchoidal) fracture surface on a thick glass edge with concentric rib (Wallner-type) ripples.
- **`refs/cat-09-conchoidal-chunk.jpg`** — [Conch fract glass](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Conch_fract_glass.jpg). Public domain; Tchenguise (A. Miserez collection). A thick glass chunk held in a hand, with conchoidal ripples on its fracture face.
- **`refs/cat-09-rib-marks-profilometer.jpg`** — [Glass Rod (5828208211)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Glass_Rod_(5828208211).jpg). Public domain; NIST. An optical profilometer height map of a glass-rod fracture surface. "Curved ribs reveal the path of the stress wave". The colours show micrometre heights.
- **`refs/cat-09-remnant-edge-in-frame.jpg`** — [Windowscape](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Windowscape_(6888074074).jpg). CC BY 2.0; Kenny Louie. The jagged fracture edge of a pane remnant still in its frame, seen at a grazing angle.
- [Conchoidally-fractured quartz 1](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Conchoidally-fractured_quartz_1.jpg). CC BY 2.0; James St. John. Conchoidal ribs on quartz, a glass-like fracture. Analogue only.
- [Glass rod fracture](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Glass_rod_fracture.jpg). CC BY-SA 3.0; Tomscience. Microscope view of the end of a broken glass stirring rod (mirror and hackle).
- [CRACK IN BOTTLE – FRACTURE STUDY OF GLASS (NARA)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:CRACK_IN_BOTTLE_-_FRACTURE_STUDY_OF_GLASS_-_NARA_-_17444881.jpg). Public domain. Microscope image of a crack origin in glass, with a scale.
- [Glass window cracks shards](https://pixabay.com/photos/glass-window-cracks-shards-broken-582689/). Pixabay Content License; TanteTati. Black and white: many long shards still in a frame, overlapping, their thickness edges visible.
- **`refs/cat-06-long-shards-edges-pexels.jpg`** (listed in 6) — green fracture-face bands on thick shards.

## 10. Edge chips

- **`refs/cat-10-edge-chips-railing-1.jpg`** — [Damaged glass 01](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Damaged_glass_01.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Kritzolina. A glass railing edge with shell-shaped conchoidal chips at the arris. The ripple lines and the green edge of the glass thickness are visible. **Key reference for chips.**
- **`refs/cat-10-edge-chips-railing-2.jpg`** — [Damaged glass 02](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Damaged_glass_02.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Kritzolina. A closer view: a fan-shaped chip scar with Wallner ripples, wider than it is deep.
- **`refs/cat-10-conchoidal-flake-flint.jpg`** — [FLAKE (FindID 1000827-1100092)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FLAKE_(FindID_1000827-1100092).jpg). CC BY 2.0; Norfolk County Council (Portable Antiquities Scheme). A struck flint flake with a scale, showing the shell shape of the chips that come off a glass edge. Analogue only.
- **`refs/cat-08-thick-shard-sidewalk.jpg`** (listed in 8) — a conchoidal broken edge on a thick shard.
- Quinn, NIST SP 960-16e3, Figs. 4.29–4.30 (pp. 4-46–4-47): chip shapes, including front views of two chips in glass. See category 16.

- **`refs/cat-11-hole-jagged.jpg`** — [Broken Window at Milwaukee Makerspace](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_Window_at_Milwaukee_Makerspace.jpg). CC BY-SA 2.0; jason gessner. A dark hole with sharp dagger points around the rim.
- **`refs/cat-11-door-hole-web-pixabay.jpg`** — [Broken glass, school, damaged window](https://pixabay.com/photos/broken-glass-school-damaged-window-1391025/). Pixabay Content License; paulsbarlow7. A door window with a missing patch and a radial and concentric web around it, cracks running to the frame.
- [Old Window Trattenbach Austria](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Old_Window_Trattenbach_Austria.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Maimaid. An old window with jagged holes in several panes.

- [Broken glass window (930160)](https://pixabay.com/photos/broken-glass-window-broken-glass-930160/). Pixabay Content License; MAKY_OREL. Black and white: an old window with a big hole and radials.

## 12. Laminated windscreen break types

The ROLAGS definitions are in `fracture-physics.md` §2.2. The best close-ups are a series by Nevit Dilmen, shot against blue sky. The glass type is not stated, but the dark separated cones are the windscreen-repair textbook look.

- **`refs/cat-12-bullseye.jpg`** — [Broken glass 1040819 Nevit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_glass_1040819_Nevit.jpg). CC BY-SA 3.0; Nevit Dilmen. **Bullseye**: a round separated cone (dark disc of air) around a crushed impact point, with nested ring cracks around it.
- **`refs/cat-12-half-moon-with-legs.jpg`** — [Broken glass 1040823 Nevit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_glass_1040823_Nevit.jpg). CC BY-SA 3.0; Nevit Dilmen. **Half-moon (partial bullseye) with legs**: a dark crescent on one side of a crushed pit, plus long straight legs.
- **`refs/cat-12-star-break.jpg`** — [Broken glass 1040822 Nevit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_glass_1040822_Nevit.jpg). CC BY-SA 3.0; Nevit Dilmen. **Star break**: a tiny pit with 6 long, thin, slightly curved legs.
- **`refs/cat-12-combination-break.jpg`** — [Broken glass 1040820 Nevit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_glass_1040820_Nevit.jpg). CC BY-SA 3.0; Nevit Dilmen. **Combination break**: a crushed core, several nested cone rings, a pale separated halo and short legs.
- **`refs/cat-12-two-bullseyes-ring-cracks.jpg`** — [Broken glass 1040824 Nevit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_glass_1040824_Nevit.jpg). CC BY-SA 3.0; Nevit Dilmen. Two bullseyes surrounded by many wide, sweeping ring and arc cracks.
- [Broken glass 1040821 Nevit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_glass_1040821_Nevit.jpg) and [1040825](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_glass_1040825_Nevit.jpg). CC BY-SA 3.0; Nevit Dilmen. 1040821 is another combination break with a pinkish crushed core. 1040825 is the two bullseyes again.
- **`refs/cat-12-star-windscreen.jpg`** — [A cracked windshield](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_cracked_windshield.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; B.H. Dhiaeddine. A windscreen star with about 8 long legs from a crushed point, seen from inside.
- **`refs/cat-12-long-crack-windscreen.jpg`** — [2015-01-29 A cracked windshield in Elko, Nevada](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:2015-01-29_08_11_14_A_cracked_windshield_in_Elko,_Nevada.JPG). CC BY-SA 4.0; Famartin. A single **long crack** curving across a windscreen.
- **`refs/cat-12-impact-with-long-cracks.jpg`** — [Scaniawindshield](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Scaniawindshield.JPG). CC BY-SA 3.0; Vcx. A truck windscreen with an impact star plus several long cracks spreading across: a combination break running into long cracks.
- [Cracked windshield (6295402403)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cracked_windshield_(6295402403).jpg). CC BY-SA 2.0; runran. An abandoned car's windscreen with a dense radial star of about 20 legs converging on a point, beaded with rain.
- [Cracked Windshield (5748324520)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cracked_Windshield_(5748324520).jpg). CC BY 2.0; Tony Webster. A van windscreen after a storm, with a large star and web, seen from inside.
- [Cracks on windshield of car on road](https://www.pexels.com/photo/cracks-on-windshield-of-car-on-road-19773544/). Pexels License; Alex Dos Santos. Black and white: a long crack across a windscreen with a small chip at one end.
- ROLAGS photo gallery ([page](https://rolags.com/proper-repairs/)), copyright NWRD with no licence stated. **(not viewed; labels from the page)** Before-and-after photos titled bullseye ([before](https://rolags.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/before_bullseye_crop_crop.jpg)), combination ([before](https://rolags.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/before_combi-1024x936.jpg)), crack ([before](https://rolags.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/crack-repair-before_1-1024x768.jpg)), large combination ([before](https://rolags.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/large-Combo_before-and-after-004_crop-1024x1014.jpg)) and star break ([before](https://rolags.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/Starbreak-before-and-after-002_crop-1024x823.jpg), [another](https://rolags.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/Star-Break-003_crop.jpg)).
- ROLAGS re-repair gallery ([page](https://rolags.com/gallery/re-repairs/)). **(not viewed)** A partial bullseye ([before](https://rolags.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/August-12-2011_Safelite_Farmers_-repair-of-a-partial-bullseye-001_crop.jpg)).
- **Not found as free images:** a clean surface pit, an edge crack and a floater crack. Use the ROLAGS definitions.

## 13. Laminated glass struck hard: spider web, held together

- **`refs/cat-13-windscreen-spiderweb.jpg`** — [Windshield-spiderweb](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Windshield-spiderweb.jpg). Public domain; Tysto. **Key reference.** A windscreen with a white crushed centre, a dense radial star and many rings, the cracks stopping well short of the edges.
- **`refs/cat-13-hail-crushed-disc.jpg`** — [FEMA 44376, truck windshield with hail damage](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FEMA_-_44376_-_truck_windshield_with_hail_damage_in_OK.jpg). Public domain; Win Henderson / FEMA. A baseball-sized hailstone left a round, white, crushed disc with radials. The sheet stayed in one piece.
- **`refs/cat-13-windscreen-star-glint.jpg`** — [EclatVerreFeuilleté](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:EclatVerreFeuillete.JPG). CC BY-SA 4.0; No-w-ay with H. Caps. Stated as a laminated windscreen. A bright crushed star at night, with radial crack faces glinting green and white.
- **`refs/cat-13-windscreen-ice-impact.jpg`** — [Autoglas gesplittert 01](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Autoglas_gesplittert_01.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Geolina163. Stated as laminated safety glass hit by an ice sheet from a lorry. A huge web of curved concentric and radial cracks, sagging but whole.
- [Autoglas gesplittert 02](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Autoglas_gesplittert_02.jpg) and [03](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Autoglas_gesplittert_03.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Geolina163. Inside views of the same windscreen.
- [Windschutzscheibe, gesplittert (2)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Windschutzscheibe,_gesplittert_(2).jpg), [(3)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Windschutzscheibe,_gesplittert_(3).jpg), [(4)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Windschutzscheibe,_gesplittert_(4).jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; 1971markus. Another laminated windscreen hit by an ice sheet: big web, rings, and cracks to the edges.
- **`refs/cat-13-shop-laminated-web.jpg`** — [Burglary attempt, jeweller, Groningen](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:20140712_Inbraakpoging_Juwelier_Verlengde_Hereweg_Groningen_NL.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Wutsje. A shop window after repeated blows: a round web with a crushed core that held, and cracks to the frame.
- **`refs/cat-13-steel-ball-star.jpg`** — [Tesla Cybertruck damaged window](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tesla_Cybertruck_damaged_window.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; u/Kruzat. A thrown steel ball made a star with a crushed centre in a laminated side window. The pane held.
- **`refs/cat-13-windscreen-sponge-grenade.jpg`** — [Windshield hit by sponge grenade](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Windshield_hit_by_sponge_grenade.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Yaron Ben-haim. A crushed crater with radials and the blue projectile stuck in it.
- **`refs/cat-13-security-glass-fan.jpg`** — [Broken-Window-20130513](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken-Window-20130513.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; WiseWoman. Captioned "Security glass does not break, but presents interesting patterns". A fan of radials from a low impact, with curved cross-cracks, all held in place.
- **`refs/cat-13-shop-window-dense-web.jpg`** — [G8 G20 Toronto 2010, smashed window on Queen St.](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:G8_G20_Toronto_2010_Smashed_Window_on_Queen_St._(4736380117).jpg). CC BY 2.0; Chris Huggins. A very dense concentric web around a crushed, nearly holed centre. Type not stated; it behaves like laminated glass.
- **`refs/cat-13-laminated-hanging.jpg`** — [Laminated safety glas vandalised 341 (part)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Laminated_safety_glas_vandalised_20060407_341_part.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Georg Slickers. A broken laminated sheet folding and hanging like cloth while staying in one piece.
- **`refs/cat-13-windscreen-head-impact-pexels.jpg`** — [Close-up of damaged car with shattered windshield](https://www.pexels.com/photo/close-up-of-damaged-car-with-shattered-windshield-30893737/). Pexels License; Alexey Veretennikov. A bull's-eye web of concentric rings on a windscreen.
- [Laminated safety glas vandalised 340](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Laminated_safety_glas_vandalised_20060407_340.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Georg Slickers. The whole sheet. Its plies look diced, so they are probably toughened.
- [Broken Laminated glass](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Broken_Laminated_glass.JPG). CC BY-SA 3.0; Ali azid. "A broken laminated glass which used in a building": a bent, crazed green sheet.
- [Bulletproof glass window after a burglary attempt](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bulletproof_glass_window_after_a_burglary_attempt.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Raimond Spekking. A jeweller's laminated security glass with several impact stars, intact.

## 15. What *not* to draw for an impact: tempered, thermal, NiS

- **`refs/cat-15-thermal-crack.jpg`** — [Temperaturni lom 2020](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Temperaturni_lom_2020.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Alek14. "Glass pane thermal break" in a balcony door: a single, smooth, curving crack from the edge, with no impact point.
- **`refs/cat-15-tempered-dice.jpg`** — [Glas zerbrochen](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Glas_zerbrochen_-_panoramio.jpg). CC BY 3.0; Kurt Spalinger-Røes. Tempered glass diced into uniform small cubes, still in place.
- **`refs/cat-15-tempered-cube-cluster.jpg`** — [EclatSécurit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:EclatSecurit.JPG). CC BY-SA 4.0; No-w-ay with H. Caps. A hand-held cluster of tempered dice.
- **`refs/cat-15-nis-butterfly.jpg`** — [Nickel sulfide inclusion glass breakage](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nickel_sulfide_inclusion_glass_breakage.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; Wolfmann, cmglee. Per the file title, a tempered pane that broke spontaneously from a nickel-sulphide inclusion: an all-over diced pattern around the origin, with no impact point.
- [Brokensafetyglasswindow](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Brokensafetyglasswindow.JPG). CC BY-SA 4.0; Mercurywoodrose. A diced tempered pane with the pavement seen through it.
- ['broken glass](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%27broken_glass.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; arivumathi. A tempered dice close-up.
- [Shattered Glass](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Shattered_Glass.jpg). CC BY-SA 4.0; ProjectManhattan. A pool seen through tempered dice.
- [Красота в Деталях](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%D0%9A%D1%80%D0%B0%D1%81%D0%BE%D1%82%D0%B0_%D0%B2_%D0%94%D0%B5%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BB%D1%8F%D1%85_(Beauty_in_details_).jpg). CC BY 4.0; Narzullaev Sukhrob. Macro of tempered granules.

CC BY-SA 3.0, Theonlysilentbob; CC BY 2.0, Angelo DeSantis. Tempered side-window granules on the ground. Compare their cube shape with the annealed daggers in category 8.
- [Car window burglary](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Car_window_burglary.jpg). CC BY-SA 3.0; Kafziel. A tempered side window with a hole and a diced rim.

CC BY-SA 4.0; Wolfmann. A 20-photo series. The pattern is diced, so the plies are toughened. This is laminated *tempered* glass, not a windscreen-type break.

## 16. Real fracture patterns in papers and guides (figures and tracings)

These are links to figures inside documents. Nothing was downloaded. They are among the most useful references because the conditions are known.

- **NIJ report 241445 (Tulleners, Thornton & Baca 2013), Appendix A, pp. A-2 to A-7** ([PDF](https://www.ojp.gov/pdffiles1/nij/grants/241445.pdf)). A US DOJ-funded grant report; copyright status not stated. **Tracings of all 60 broken 203 mm, 3 mm window panes**, 10 per condition:
  - drop weight with blunt, round or sharp tip (A-2 to A-4);
  - slow press in a frame (A-5 to A-7).
  - **The single best answer to "repetitive and too consistent".**
  - Report Figs. 10–15 (pp. 32–35) are larger examples. The round-tip star is about 20 radials. The sharp-tip pattern has lens-shaped pieces. The blunt-tip fan comes from an edge. The pressed panes have more than 100 radials with ring bands and a central hole.
- **Quinn, NIST SP 960-16e3** ([PDF](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/NIST.SP.960-16e3.pdf)). A US Government work; individual figures are credited to the people named. PDF page in brackets.
  - Fig. 4.17b (p. 4-26 [131]): a real window broken by a deer. Very many radials, with a dense band of short concentric segments around the impact.
  - Fig. 4.20 (p. 4-32 [137]): sketches of window fracture patterns: ball impact, centre impact with secondary ring cracks, sharp and blunt impacts, pressure-loaded plates.
  - Fig. 4.15 (p. 4-22 [127]): fan arrays and inner and outer cross-cracks in disks.
  - Fig. 4.21 (p. 4-34 [139]): tempered car windows. For comparison only.
  - Figs. 4.22–4.23 (p. 4-35 [140]): thermal cracks that start at the edge and wave.
  - Figs. 4.29–4.30 (pp. 4-46–4-47 [151–152]): edge chips, including in glass.
  - Figs. 5.32–5.34 (pp. 5-45–5-47): twist hackle in glass.
  - Fig. 6.33 (p. 6-37 [305]): sharp-impact origins in glass, pulverised, with concentric Wallner lines.
  - Fig. 6.36 (p. 6-39 [307]): cone profiles for static, oblique, sliding and impact loading.
  - Fig. 6.39 (p. 6-43 [311]): real blunt-impact cones in glass plates. In (a) the plate survived with nested ring cones. In (b) there is a cone plus radials and a scalloped crater.
- **Kim et al. 2025**, *Appl. Sci.* 15:386 ([article](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/15/1/386)), CC BY 4.0. Figs. 4–5: cone cracks and holes in 4.8 mm float glass from 8 and 10 mm steel balls at a range of speeds.
- **Kim 2025**, *Appl. Sci.* 15:10898 ([article](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/15/20/10898)), CC BY. Figs. 2–3: cone cracks and holes at impact angles from 0 to 80°.
- **Lux et al. 2022**, *Int. J. Legal Med.* ([article](https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00414-022-02904-z)), CC BY 4.0. Figures of shots through laminated windscreen glass and the "compounded fragments" of glass grit on punched-out PVB discs.
- **Wang et al. 2024**, *Int. J. Fract.* ([accepted manuscript](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10597886)); publisher copyright. Fig. 1: strike and back faces of a 3.3 mm glass plate hit at 150 m/s. Fig. 4: roughness on a cone-crack chip.
- **ASTM C1256** ([copy](https://elitesafetyglass.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/ASTM-C1256-Standard-Practice-for-Interpreting-Glass-Fracture-Surface-Features.pdf)); ASTM copyright. Figs. 1–13: mirror, mist, Wallner lines, hackle, twist hackle, cantilever curl.
- **Zemanová et al. 2020**, Challenging Glass Conference ([PDF](https://proceedings.challengingglass.com/index.php/cgc/article/download/319/300/898)); authors' copyright. Photos of laminated plates after drop tests, showing the X-shaped band of radials.

---

**Searched but thin on free images.** These do not appear on Wikimedia Commons under these names: "Cracked glass" (empty), "Bullet holes in glass", "Fractography" of glass, "Wallner lines" and "Windshield damage". The Commons "Fractography" category is almost all metals.

**Glass type is often unknown.** Shop windows and doors photographed broken are often laminated or tempered. For annealed-only references, prefer:

- the domestic window shots (`cat-01-small-star-near-frame`, `cat-08-fallen-pane-star`, `cat-08-flat-shards-paving`);
- the NIJ tracings;
- Quinn Fig. 4.17b.
